Lung cancer is a hard cancer to treat, and many people still die from it (Abstract, sentence 1). Even with new drugs and chemo, most people with lung cancer do not live five years after they learn they have it (Abstract, sentence 2). So we need better treatment choices for you and others with this disease (Abstract, sentence 2). Bispecific antibodies are special because they can grab onto two different targets at the same time (Abstract, sentence 3). In this study, the team read and summed up many past studies to explain how these drugs are built and how they work in the body (Abstract, sentence 6). They also looked at how far these drugs have gone in tests with people who have lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 6). The team found that three of these drugs are now approved to treat lung cancer, which shows they can help some patients (Abstract, sentence 4). Many more of these drugs are now in human tests to check how safe they are and how well they work (Abstract, sentence 5). These findings may guide doctors and drug makers as they plan new lung cancer care in the future (Abstract, sentence 6).

Title: Updates on lung cancer screening for early detection.
Abstract: This review examines the current status and recent progress in lung cancer screening programs, focusing on low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) and emerging liquid biopsy technologies. In Korea, the National Lung Cancer Screening Program has shown promising results in reducing lung cancer mortality since its implementation in 2019. This review discusses the LDCT screening in Korea, including reductions in short-term mortality, increased screening uptake, and enhanced smoking cessation rates. Results from major international trials, including the National Lung Screening Trial, Nederlands-Leuvens Longkanker Screenings Onderzoek trial, and Multicenter Italian Lung Detection studies, demonstrating the efficacy of LDCT in reducing lung cancer mortality, are reviewed. The potential of liquid biopsy as a complement to LDCT is explored, with a focus on multi-cancer early detection technologies. Notable advances include the Circulating Cell-free Genome Atlas study and the Galleri® test, which have shown promise in detecting cancer at early stages through blood-based screening. We also highlight the challenges and limitations of current screening methods, including the need to improve strategies for screening non-smokers and the importance of balancing benefits against risks. As lung cancer screening continues to advance, combining LDCT and liquid biopsy is anticipated to provide more comprehensive and effective early detection strategies.

It talks about a scan called low‑dose CT and new blood tests that may help find cancer (Abstract, sentence 1). We need this study because lung cancer often shows up late, when it is hard to treat (Abstract, sentence 4). It may help people who smoke now or smoked in the past, and may later help people who never smoked (Abstract, sentence 7). The team looked at past large trials from many countries to see how well the scan works (Abstract, sentence 4). They also looked at new blood tests that search for tiny bits of cancer in the blood (Abstract, sentence 5). They found that the scan can lower deaths from lung cancer in big groups of people (Abstract, sentence 4). In Korea, a national scan plan that began in 2019 has cut short‑term deaths and helped more people join scans and quit smoking (Abstract, sentence 2). New blood tests, like the Galleri test, can sometimes find cancer early from a blood draw (Abstract, sentence 6). These results matter because early find can mean more time and more treatment choices (Abstract, sentence 3). In the future, using both the scan and a blood test together may give a stronger way to find lung cancer early (Abstract, sentence 8).

Title: CircRNA in non‑small cell lung cancer: Potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets (Review).
Abstract: Lung cancer is one of the most common malignant tumors, characterized by high incidence and mortality rates. Non‑small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the predominant histological type of lung cancer. Due to the lack of effective early diagnostic methods, the majority of patients with lung cancer present with distant metastasis at the time of initial diagnosis, often rendering treatments such as surgery and pharmacotherapy ineffective. Consequently, there is an urgent need for a more in‑depth understanding of the pathogenesis of NSCLC and the identification of novel therapeutic targets to enable more precise prediction and treatment of the disease. circular RNAs (circRNAs) are specifically expressed in tissues, owing to their high stability and specificity. The dysregulation of circRNA expression has been implicated in cancer progression, where circRNAs function as microRNA sponges, RNA‑binding protein sponges, gene splicing and transcriptional regulators and protein/peptide translational modulators. These molecules may serve as potential biomarkers for cancer prognosis and predictive indicators, as well as novel therapeutic targets. The present review summarizes the biogenesis and mechanistic functions of circRNAs, outlines their potential role in the initiation and progression of NSCLC and discusses their application as therapeutic targets in cancer treatment. The present review aimed to provide new perspectives for the development of emerging diagnostic or prognostic biomarkers and potential therapeutic targets for NSCLC.

Many people learn they have lung cancer only after it has spread far in the body, so surgery and drugs often do not work well (Abstract, sentence 3). The writers of this paper wanted to better understand how NSCLC starts and grows, so that we can find new ways to test and treat it (Abstract, sentence 4). They did not run a new lab test on people, but instead read and summed up many past studies (Abstract, sentence 8). The paper says these ring pieces may work as signs in the blood or tissue to help tell how the cancer may act and how a person may do over time (Abstract, sentence 7). The authors hope this work will guide new tests to find NSCLC earlier and new drug targets to treat it better in the future (Abstract, sentence 9).

The authors read and summed up many lab and animal studies that measured circRNAs in lung tumors and normal tissue [E16]. They looked at how these ring molecules control cancer cell growth, spread, and how the body’s defense cells react to the tumor [E15].  

They found that some circRNAs act like “on” switches that help lung cancer cells grow and move, while others act like “off” switches that slow or block the cancer [E17]. Certain circRNAs also help cancer cells hide from the immune system or resist drugs, while others make drug treatment work better [E20].  

These results matter because stable circRNAs in blood or other body fluids may serve as early warning signs or as new drug targets for NSCLC in the future [E25]. With better testing tools, circRNAs may one day help guide more exact, person‑specific lung cancer care [E29].

Title: Lactylation modification in lung cancer: A review of current research and future directions (Review).
Abstract: Lung cancer is a common malignancy that poses risks to human health and quality of life. The primary treatment options currently available include surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy. However, the aggressive metastatic nature of the disease combined with the development of drug and radiation resistance results in suboptimal survival outcomes. Consequently, there is a need to explore novel therapeutic approaches and develop more effective drugs. Lactylation, an epigenetic modification induced by lactate, alters histone proteins to modify the chromatin structure, as well as non‑histone proteins. This post‑translational modification is associated with the initiation and progression of lung cancer. Lactylation carries out a considerable role in the onset, progression and resistance of the disease by influencing tumor metabolism and the surrounding microenvironment. Targeting lactylation could provide innovative strategies for the targeted therapy of lung cancer.
Abstract_Summary: This study looks at lung cancer, which is a very common and serious type of cancer that harms health and daily life (Abstract, sentence 1). Right now, you may get surgery, drug treatment, or radiation for lung cancer, but these do not always work well because the cancer can spread and stop responding to these treatments (Abstract, sentence 2). This means many people still do not live as long as we want, so we need new and better ways to treat this disease (Abstract, sentence 3)(Abstract, sentence 4). The researchers looked at a small change in cells called “lactylation,” which is caused by a substance called lactate (Abstract, sentence 5). This change can affect key cell parts and how the cell’s “control center” is packed and used (Abstract, sentence 5). They found that this change is linked to how lung cancer starts, grows, and becomes hard to treat (Abstract, sentence 6). It also seems to affect how the tumor uses energy and how it acts with nearby cells (Abstract, sentence 7). The study suggests that if we can block or change lactylation, we may be able to create new, more exact drugs for lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 8). In the future, this might give people with lung cancer more treatment choices and better care (Abstract, sentence 8).

Title: Ferroptosis and Radiotherapy in Lung Cancer.
Abstract: BACKGROUND: Lung cancer (LC) is a leading cause of cancer mortality worldwide. While radiotherapy (RT) has been a lasting cornerstone of LC management, there are concerns due to tumor radioresistance and unintended damage to surrounding healthy tissue. Ferroptosis is a recently described mechanism of programmed cell death which has potential to serve as a complementary adjunct to facilitate RT-based LC treatment. OBJECTIVES: This review is a comprehensive overview of ferroptosis in the broader context of synergism with RT for LC. SUMMARY: Ferroptosis is essentially driven by intracellular iron overload, which drives the formation of reactive oxygen species, ultimately resulting in membrane instability and cell death. LC lines have been shown to exhibit a heterogeneous mix of pro- and anti-ferroptotic changes. RT shows promise as a potential ferroptosis inducer, especially when complemented with pharmacologic agents such as erastin. CONCLUSIONS: Ferroptosis represents a promising modern adjunct to a traditional therapeutic strategy. Future work should focus on rigorous dosage standards to avoid unintended toxicity, repurposing of currently available drugs into ferroptosis inducers, and establishment of safety protocols to begin the pathway towards clinical studies.
Abstract_Summary: This research looks at lung cancer and a new way to help kill cancer cells called ferroptosis (Abstract, sentence 1). We need this study because lung cancer is a major cause of death, and while we use radiation to treat it, the cancer can resist the rays and nearby healthy tissue can get hurt (Abstract, sentence 1). The writers of this paper read and summed up many lab studies that test how ferroptosis works with radiation in lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 4). They explain that ferroptosis is a kind of planned cell death that happens when iron builds up inside a cell and makes harmful forms of oxygen, which then break the cell’s outer skin and cause the cell to die (Abstract, sentence 5). They found that lung cancer cells can show both signs that make ferroptosis easier and signs that block it, so the mix is not the same in all cells (Abstract, sentence 6). They also found that radiation can help start ferroptosis, and this effect may grow stronger when we add some drugs, such as a drug called erastin (Abstract, sentence 7). These results suggest that ferroptosis may be a useful add-on to standard radiation for lung cancer (Abstract, sentence 8). Future work needs to set safe dose rules and test if some old drugs can be used to trigger ferroptosis in people (Abstract, sentence 9).
